name: Lupus miliaris disseminatus faciei
aliases: FIGURE (facial idiopathic granulomas with regressive evolution)

clinicalPearls: Presents with crops of monomorphic reddish-brown to yellowish dome-shaped papules symmetrically distributed over the central face
The eyelids and periocular region are characteristically involved, and lesions may cluster around the lower eyelids and upper cheeks
Diascopy typically shows an apple-jelly colour, reflecting the underlying dermal granulomata
Histology reveals dermal epithelioid granulomata that frequently show central caseation-like necrosis, once causing confusion with a tuberculid
It is now regarded as an idiopathic granulomatous disorder unrelated to tuberculosis, despite the historical name
The condition is self-limiting but often persists for months to years and characteristically resolves with pitted or depressed scars
Its relationship to granulomatous rosacea is debated, and the two share overlapping clinical and histological features
Management is difficult and largely empirical, using oral tetracyclines and other systemic agents while avoiding potent topical corticosteroids
reference.pathophysiology: The cause of lupus miliaris disseminatus faciei is unknown. It is characterised by dermal granulomatous inflammation, classically epithelioid granulomata with central caseation-like necrosis, arising in a symmetrical facial distribution. Although the historical name and the necrotising histology suggested a tuberculid, no consistent link to mycobacterial infection has been demonstrated, and tuberculin reactions and mycobacterial studies are typically negative. It is now considered an idiopathic granulomatous reaction pattern, possibly related to a follicular or perifollicular process, and is discussed alongside granulomatous rosacea as part of a shared spectrum. The tendency to scar reflects destruction of dermal structures by the granulomatous infiltrate.
additionalDifferentials: Perioral (periorificial) dermatitis, including its granulomatous form
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy demonstrating caseating epithelioid granulomata
Mycobacterial stains, culture and molecular testing to exclude tuberculosis
Investigations for sarcoidosis, including chest imaging, when granulomata are found
Tuberculin or interferon-gamma release testing to help exclude active tuberculosis
Assessment of Demodex density where clinically relevant
Review of previous topical corticosteroid exposure as an aggravating factor
redFlags: Necrotising facial granulomata requiring exclusion of tuberculosis before immunosuppression
Rapidly progressive or ulcerating lesions atypical for the condition
Periocular involvement threatening the eyelids or ocular surface
Development of disfiguring scarring during the active phase
reference.prognosis: The disorder is self-limiting and usually resolves spontaneously over one to two years, but it frequently leaves permanent pitted or depressed scars, and treatment often produces only modest benefit.
pitfalls: Being misled by the caseating histology into diagnosing tuberculosis without supporting microbiology
Using potent topical corticosteroids, which tend to aggravate the eruption
Delaying treatment and allowing avoidable scarring to develop
Overlooking sarcoidosis as an alternative cause of facial granulomata
references: British Association of Dermatologists clinical guidance
